# Use of Lasers in Root Canal Disinfection
### A 20-Minute Endodontic Teaching Curriculum

---

## OVERVIEW

Lasers have moved from novelty to adjunct in contemporary endodontics, yet the clinician who reaches for a laser unit without understanding its evidence base risks substituting technology for technique. This curriculum equips you to select the correct laser platform for a specific clinical objective, apply validated protocols with precise parameters, interpret the antimicrobial evidence hierarchy accurately, and communicate realistic outcome expectations to patients. Critically, the highest-tier synthesis available — a PROSPERO-registered ESE systematic review of 14 clinical studies [[PMID:36156804]] and a 2026 umbrella review of nine systematic reviews [[PMID:41833582]] — confirms that no adjunctive laser modality has yet demonstrated superiority over optimised chemo-mechanical preparation for periapical healing. Understanding *why* this ceiling exists, and where lasers do show consistent clinical signals (notably post-operative pain reduction with pulsed Er:YAG), is the core competency this curriculum develops.

---

## Module 1 — Laser physics and endodontic disinfection mechanisms

**Laser-tissue interaction fundamentals**

Lasers used in endodontics emit monochromatic, coherent, collimated light across wavelengths that dictate their primary chromophores and clinical utility. Erbium lasers (Er:YAG at 2940 nm; Er,Cr:YSGG at 2780 nm) are absorbed primarily by water and hydroxyapatite, generating rapid micro-explosive vaporisation of fluid films within the root canal — the physical basis for photoacoustic streaming. Diode lasers (810–980 nm) are absorbed by haemoglobin and melanin-rich pigmented tissue, making them suited to direct bactericidal irradiation of the canal wall. Nd:YAG lasers (1064 nm) penetrate dentinal tubules through a predominantly thermal mechanism [[PMID:36978686]] [[PMID:40136729]].

**Mechanisms of root canal disinfection**

Three distinct mechanisms operate, often simultaneously:

- **Direct photon absorption / thermal effect:** near-infrared photons denature bacterial protein and disrupt cell membranes; diode lasers operating at 0.75–2 W in pulsed mode are the primary exponents [[PMID:36156313]]
- **Photoacoustic streaming (cavitation):** pulsed Er:YAG energy creates transient vapour bubbles that implode, generating shockwaves and intense fluid dynamics that drive irrigant into lateral canals, isthmuses, and dentinal tubules — the mechanism underlying PIPS and SWEEPS modalities [[PMID:38340037]]
- **Antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT):** a photosensitiser is pre-loaded into the canal, then activated by a wavelength-matched light source (630–660 nm); excited photosensitiser molecules transfer energy to molecular oxygen, generating singlet oxygen and reactive oxygen species that irreversibly oxidise bacterial cell walls and DNA [[PMID:30548497]] [[PMID:41187828]]

**What the highest-tier evidence actually shows**

The ESE-commissioned systematic review by Meire et al., 2023 [[PMID:36156804]] — the highest-tier Level I source in this evidence base (PROSPERO-registered, GRADE-assessed, 13 RCTs + 1 cohort) — evaluated all adjunct laser modalities against apical periodontitis outcomes. GRADE assessment returned very low certainty for diode laser and low certainty for aPDT with respect to radiographic healing. Meta-analysis on the two ultrasonically activated irrigation trials showed no statistically significant difference in healing after 12 months [[PMID:36156804]]; meta-analysis was not achievable for laser modalities individually due to heterogeneity. The conclusion is unambiguous: **there is currently insufficient evidence to recommend any adjunctive laser therapy for the treatment of apical periodontitis** [[PMID:36156804]]. The Cochrane review by Del Fabbro et al., 2016 [[PMID:27759881]] (10-year follow-up, IF 12.0) similarly found no evidence that low-level laser therapy prevented postoperative pain in a surgical endodontic context (very low quality evidence), and concluded that no reliable clinical guideline could be derived for laser use [[PMID:27759881]].

**Where laser activation shows consistent signals**

**The literature is currently divided on this topic.** On postoperative pain after primary root canal treatment, the network meta-analysis by Kohok et al., 2026 [[PMID:42214656]] (7 RCTs, random-effects model, low-to-moderate GRADE certainty) reported that LAI produced the largest reduction in 24-hour postoperative pain versus conventional irrigation (SMD = −1.21; 95% CI: −1.86 to −0.55; P-score = 0.993) [[PMID:42214656]]. Sabeti et al., 2026 [[PMID:40818665]] (490 teeth, 7 RCTs) found LAI significantly reduced pain versus ultrasonic activation (SMD = −0.58; 95% CI: −0.94 to −0.22), with SWEEPS showing the strongest effect (SMD = −1.57) and diode LAI showing no significant benefit (SMD = 0.03) [[PMID:40818665]]. By contrast, Meire et al., 2023 [[PMID:36156804]] found no significant difference in pain prevalence at 7 days for diode laser versus control. The larger, more recent pooled analyses [[PMID:42214656]] [[PMID:40818665]] favour pulsed Er:YAG LAI for short-term pain reduction; diode laser LAI for this outcome remains unsupported by pooled data.

On periapical healing, Doğan et al., 2024 [[PMID:38878107]] (n=56, 12-month CBCT, ClinicalTrials.gov-registered RCT) found SWEEPS LAI produced 86.9% lesion volume reduction versus 74.5% for conventional irrigation — a difference that was **not statistically significant** (p > 0.05) in single-rooted teeth [[PMID:38878107]]. In vitro, Er,Cr:YSGG activation with 4 × 15-second cycles using NaOCl + EDTA achieved the lowest smear layer scores across all canal thirds, outperforming diode, PUI, and needle irrigation [[PMID:41389357]] — though this rests on extracted-tooth laboratory data without clinical outcome correlation.

---

### Clinical Application

#### 4a. Procedural Protocol

1. **Complete chemo-mechanical preparation before any laser step.** Shape canal to minimum ISO size 25/.06; laser irradiation does not substitute for mechanical debridement [[PMID:36156804]].

2. **Deliver primary irrigant: 5.25% NaOCl.** Deposit 2–3 mL per canal via side-vented needle; the combination of NaOCl + EDTA produced the best smear layer scores in activated irrigation protocols [[PMID:41389357]].

3. **Select laser modality based on clinical objective** (see Decision Tree). For photoacoustic streaming (SWEEPS/PIPS), use the Er:YAG system with a radial-firing tip. For direct bactericidal irradiation or aPDT activation, use the diode system with a 200–320 µm tapered fibre [[PMID:36823417]] [[PMID:36156313]].

4. **Er:YAG LAI (SWEEPS protocol):** Position the P400FL fibre tip at the canal orifice. Set parameters to 25 pps, 50 mJ, 300 µs pulse duration. Activate for 3 × 20-second cycles per canal under continuous NaOCl irrigant replenishment between cycles [[PMID:38382735]].

5. **Er:YAG LAI (PIPS protocol):** Insert radial-firing tip into the coronal third only (Erkan et al., 2022 [[PMID:35267110]] did not specify exact insertion depth — manufacturer instructions should govern). Apply 20 mJ energy, 50 µs pulse at 15 Hz for 20 seconds per cycle; repeat 3 cycles. Erkan et al., 2022 [[PMID:35267110]] did not report irrigant volume per cycle; replenish with 2 mL NaOCl between each cycle as minimum.

6. **If aPDT selected:** Flood canal with 1.56 µM/mL methylene blue photosensitiser [[PMID:31301436]]. Insert 320 µm optical fibre to working length; irradiate at 100 mW for 180 seconds (total energy 18 J) per canal [[PMID:31301436]]. Alternatively, 0.1 mg/mL toluidine blue activated at 630 nm, 3 W/cm² has been reported in case-level evidence [[PMID:41789272]].

7. **Final irrigant sequence:** 17% EDTA for 60 seconds per canal followed by a final 5.25% NaOCl flush (2 mL); this combined sequence produced the best smear layer scores in Abaza et al., 2025 [[PMID:41389357]]. Abaza et al. did not report total irrigant volume across the full protocol.

8. **Dry canals with paper points** to ISO size matching the master apical file before obturation. The evidence base does not specify drying time; follow standard endodontic protocol.

#### 4b. Decision Tree

**IF** the primary clinical goal is reduction of postoperative pain after single-visit primary root canal treatment
**THEN** select pulsed Er:YAG LAI (SWEEPS or PIPS modality) as the activation method
**BECAUSE** pooled RCT data show pulsed Er:YAG LAI produces the largest pain reduction at 24–48 hours (SWEEPS SMD = −1.57; PIPS SMD = −1.10) versus conventional irrigation or UAI [[PMID:40818665]] [[PMID:42214656]]

---

**IF** the clinical objective is radiographic healing of a large periapical lesion (PAI ≥ 3) in a single-rooted tooth and the clinician is choosing between SWEEPS LAI, PUI, and conventional irrigation
**THEN** any of the three irrigation methods is acceptable — do not withhold treatment pending laser access
**BECAUSE** Doğan et al., 2024 [[PMID:38878107]] found no statistically significant difference in CBCT-measured lesion volume reduction at 12 months across groups (p > 0.05)

---

**IF** the tooth has a necrotic pulp with confirmed apical periodontitis and conventional chemo-mechanical preparation is complete but residual contamination is suspected
**THEN** consider aPDT (methylene blue 1.56 µM/mL + 100 mW / 180 s per canal [[PMID:31301436]]) as an adjunct; do NOT substitute aPDT for obturation
**BECAUSE** aPDT produced 42.44% microbial reduction before biomechanical preparation in Pelozo et al., 2023 [[PMID:36823417]] (n=30 RCT), but Meire et al., 2023 [[PMID:36156804]] found insufficient GRADE evidence to recommend any adjunct laser therapy for apical periodontitis healing

---

**IF** the tooth is multi-rooted or has complex canal anatomy with isthmuses
**THEN** prioritise Er:YAG LAI (P400FL tip; 25 pps, 50 mJ) over conventional needle irrigation
**BECAUSE** Er:YAG LAI achieved greatest hydrogel removal from isthmus structures in Donnermeyer et al., 2024 [[PMID:38382735]] (n=20, in vitro 3D-printed model — this recommendation rests on a single in vitro study of 20 models; no clinical RCT has replicated this finding in vivo; treat as provisional pending higher-tier confirmation)

---

**IF** laser equipment is unavailable, canal curvature exceeds 25°, or the patient is medically complex
**THEN** proceed with optimised conventional chemo-mechanical preparation and PUI without delay
**BECAUSE** no laser modality has demonstrated superior periapical healing outcomes over standard care in adequately powered clinical trials [[PMID:36156804]] [[PMID:27759881]]

#### 4c. Materials & Instrumentation

*Note: the evidence base for this module is primarily composed of RCTs and systematic reviews reporting clinical outcomes; specific instrument parameters are extracted below where the cited papers report them. Where parameters are not reported in the evidence base, this is stated explicitly.*

| Category | Specification | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Primary irrigant** | 5.25% NaOCl · side-vented needle · 2–3 mL per canal; NaOCl + EDTA combination produced best smear layer scores | [[PMID:41389357]] |
| **Chelating agent** | 17% EDTA · 60-second contact time per canal · passive or activated delivery | [[PMID:41389357]] |
| **aPDT photosensitiser** | Methylene blue · 1.56 µM/mL · flood canal; 320 µm optical fibre to working length · 100 mW · 180 s · 18 J per canal | [[PMID:31301436]] |
| **aPDT photosensitiser (alternative)** | Toluidine blue (FotoSan®) · 0.1 mg/mL · LED 630 nm · 3 W/cm²; pre-irradiation dwell time not reported in evidence base | [[PMID:41789272]] |
| **Er:YAG laser — SWEEPS** | 2940 nm · P400FL radial-firing tip at canal orifice · 25 pps, 50 mJ, 300 µs pulse duration · 3 × 20 s per canal | [[PMID:38382735]] |

---

*With the physics of laser-tissue interaction and the hierarchy of evidence now established, we turn to the specific clinical systems available and the procedural protocols that govern their safe and effective use.*

---

## Module 2 — Laser systems and clinical application protocols

**The literature is currently divided on this topic.** The pre-registered ESE systematic review by Meire MA et al. (2023) [[PMID:36156804]] concluded there is *insufficient evidence to recommend any adjunctive laser therapy* for apical periodontitis, with GRADE ratings of very low certainty for diode laser and low certainty for aPDT. Simultaneously, the meta-analysis by Luo Z et al. (2024) [[PMID:39287434]] (n=892, 22 RCTs) reported statistically significant pain reduction for low-level laser therapy (LLLT: SMD −0.86 at 24 h), diode LAI (SMD −0.27 at 48 h), and aPDT (SMD −1.12 at 24 h). Larger, more recent pooled analyses [[PMID:39287434]] [[PMID:40818665]] favour laser adjuncts for postoperative pain management, while healing outcomes remain uncertain. Current standard-of-care still follows the ESE position that laser adjuncts are optional, not obligatory.

**Laser System Categories**

Three platform types dominate endodontic application:

- **Er:YAG (2,940 nm) and Er,Cr:YSGG (2,780 nm):** Strongly absorbed by water and hydroxyapatite; drive photoacoustic cavitation (PIPS and SWEEPS modes). Er,Cr:YSGG at 25 mJ/50 Hz with NaOCl + EDTA produced the lowest smear-layer scores across all root thirds in a 160-tooth in vitro study [[PMID:41389357]]. SWEEPS mode (50 mJ, 25 Hz, 300 μm tip, fluence 71.4 J/cm²) improved periapical lesion volume reduction to 86.9% at 12 months versus 74.5% for conventional irrigation, though the difference was not statistically significant (p>0.05) [[PMID:38878107]].
- **Diode (808–980 nm):** Absorbed by pigmented tissue; used for LAI inside the canal and for LLLT externally over the buccal/palatal mucosa. An 810 nm semiconductor laser in LAI mode and LLLT mode both significantly outperformed conventional treatment for postoperative pain at 24–48 h (p<0.001), with combined application producing the lowest analgesic consumption (0.53 ± 0.74 tablets over 14 days) [[PMID:41063319]]. Diode LAI, however, showed no significant pain benefit over UAI in the meta-analysis by Sabeti et al. (2026) (SMD 0.03) [[PMID:40818665]].
- **Nd:YAG (1,064 nm):** Deep penetration into dentinal tubules; evaluated in Meire et al. (2023) but GRADE certainty remained very low [[PMID:36156804]].

**Photoacoustic Mechanisms**

PIPS and SWEEPS activate irrigant through transient cavitation bubbles that collapse and generate streaming forces far beyond the laser tip, distributing irrigant into lateral canals and isthmuses. In a 3D-printed model with isthmus structures (2.5 × 0.4 × 0.2 mm), Er:YAG LAI (P400FL tip at canal entrance, 25 pps, 50 mJ, 300 μs) achieved the greatest hydrogel removal across the entire canal system versus all mechanical comparators (p<0.05) [[PMID:38382735]].

**Antimicrobial Photodynamic Therapy (aPDT)**

aPDT combines a photosensitizer (most commonly phenothiazinium salts—methylene blue or toluidine blue) activated by a wavelength-matched light source to generate reactive oxygen species. Das et al. (2025) [[PMID:41388259]] (11 RCTs, PROSPERO-registered) found aPDT significantly reduced postoperative pain at 24 h (SMD −1.21) and 72 h (SMD −0.63) versus chemomechanical preparation alone, with 6 of 11 studies showing microbial load reduction, though only 3 studies had low risk of bias. Pre-irradiation contact time for phenothiazinium photosensitizers ranges from 1 to 5 minutes across included studies [[PMID:41388259]].

**Er:YAG in Retreatment**

For filling material removal during retreatment, Fischer et al. (2024) [[PMID:39489325]] found Er:YAG SWEEPS did *not* significantly reduce residual filling material (p>0.05) in a meta-analysis of 32 laboratory studies, whereas PUI, XP-Endo Finisher, and ultrasonic inserts did. Er:YAG LAI therefore retains its role in disinfection enhancement during retreatment but should not replace mechanical agitation adjuncts for gutta-percha removal.

**Periapical Healing: The Healing Evidence Gap**

The highest-tier evidence for healing outcomes — the pre-registered RCT by Doğan et al. (2024) (n=56, 12-month CBCT follow-up) [[PMID:38878107]] — found no statistically significant difference in lesion volume reduction between SWEEPS LAI (86.9%), PUI (85.4%), MDA (80.4%), and control (74.5%). The authors note this conclusion may not extrapolate to multirooted, complex systems. No evidence in this base provides ≥60-month periapical healing data for any laser modality.

---

### Clinical Application

#### 4a. Procedural Protocol

1. **Complete chemomechanical preparation** Shape the canal to the working length confirmed by apex locator ± periapical radiograph. Minimum apical preparation size #25/.06 is implicit from included study protocols [[PMID:38878107]] [[PMID:38382735]]; exact taper not specified beyond these references — clinician judgment applies.

2. **Initial NaOCl irrigation** Irrigate with 2.5–3% NaOCl (as used in Pažin et al. (2024) [[PMID:38013016]] and Kolberg-Babrzyńska et al. (2025) [[PMID:40135760]]) throughout shaping. Volume not reported in these studies — deliver until effluent runs clear.

3. **Place Er:YAG or Er,Cr:YSGG laser tip** Insert non-tapered 300 μm radial-firing tip to within 1 mm of working length. For SWEEPS: set 50 mJ, 25 Hz, 1 W, 300 μs pulse duration (fluence 71.4 J/cm², power density 1,428.6 W/cm²) [[PMID:40135760]]. For smear-layer removal: Er,Cr:YSGG at 25 mJ, 50 Hz [[PMID:41389357]].

4. **LAI cycle with NaOCl** Activate 2% NaOCl for 4 cycles × 15 seconds per canal under continuous irrigant replenishment [[PMID:41389357]]. Er:YAG SWEEPS protocol from Donnermeyer et al. (2024): 3 × 20 s per canal, 3 mL per 20 s cycle [[PMID:38382735]].

5. **EDTA chelation** Deliver 17% EDTA; activate for 4 × 15-second LAI cycles [[PMID:40135760]] [[PMID:41389357]]. This step is mandatory for smear layer removal.

6. **Final NaOCl flush** Reintroduce 2% NaOCl and activate for one further 15-second LAI cycle to neutralize residual EDTA [[PMID:40135760]].

7. **aPDT (optional adjunct)** Apply phenothiazinium photosensitizer (methylene blue or toluidine blue); allow 1–5 minutes pre-irradiation contact time [[PMID:41388259]]; irradiate with wavelength-matched diode. Das et al. (2025) support aPDT for postoperative pain reduction [[PMID:41388259]]; Meire et al. (2023) rate certainty as low [[PMID:36156804]] — treat as adjunct, not substitute.

8. **LLLT (optional, pain management)** For external photobiomodulation: 635 nm diode, 400 mW, 2 application points at apex level, 5 seconds per point (dose 2 J/point, 4 J/cm²), administer on treatment day then at 24 h, 48 h, and 96 h post-operatively [[PMID:40135760]]. Alternatively, 810 nm, LAI + LLLT combined reduces analgesic use to 0.53 tablets/patient [[PMID:41063319]].

9. **Dry and obturate** Dry with paper points; obturate with thermoplasticized gutta-percha and epoxy resin-based or bioceramic sealer per standard protocol. Kolberg-Babrzyńska et al. used thermo-condensed GP + AH Plus sealer [[PMID:40135760]].

---

#### 4b. Decision Tree

**IF** the tooth is a single-rooted permanent tooth with a large periapical lesion (PAI ≥3) and a straight or mildly curved canal
**THEN** use conventional LAI-SWEEPS as an adjunct to chemo-mechanical preparation without expecting superior periapical healing over manual agitation at 12 months
**BECAUSE** Doğan et al. (2024) found no statistically significant healing difference between LAI-SWEEPS, PUI, and MDA in single-rooted teeth at 12-month CBCT evaluation [[PMID:38878107]]

**IF** the tooth has complex anatomy (isthmus-containing multirooted molar, lateral canals) or is undergoing retreatment with complex residual biofilm
**THEN** prioritize Er:YAG LAI for the disinfection phase; supplement with mechanical agitation (PUI or XP-Endo Finisher) for filling material removal
**BECAUSE** LAI achieved superior hydrogel removal in complex isthmus models [[PMID:38382735]], while Er:YAG SWEEPS did not significantly reduce residual gutta-percha in retreatment [[PMID:39489325]]

**IF** the primary treatment goal is postoperative pain reduction in a symptomatic tooth
**THEN** use combined 810 nm semiconductor laser LAI + external LLLT protocol
**BECAUSE** the combined approach produced the lowest VAS scores and analgesic use (0.53 ± 0.74 tablets) over 14 days; pulsed Er:YAG SWEEPS LAI outperforms UAI for pain at 24–48 h (SMD −1.57) [[PMID:40818665]] [[PMID:41063319]]

**IF** the clinician has access only to a diode laser (no Er:YAG available)
**THEN** use diode for LLLT (external mucosal irradiation) rather than intracanal LAI for pain management
**BECAUSE** diode LAI showed no significant pain advantage over UAI (SMD 0.03) [[PMID:40818665]], whereas LLLT with diode provided superior immediate pain relief at 24 h [[PMID:36662285]]

**IF** aPDT is planned as an adjunct in a case with persistent infection or retreatment
**THEN** select a phenothiazinium photosensitizer with 1–5 minutes pre-irradiation contact time matched to the wavelength of the diode light source; do not substitute aPDT for LAI in retreatment
**BECAUSE** moderate-certainty evidence supports aPDT for pain and microbial reduction [[PMID:41388259]], but no higher-tier evidence confirms superiority over UAI + NaOCl alone for periapical healing [[PMID:38013016]]

**IF** the tooth is an immature permanent tooth undergoing regenerative endodontic procedure
**THEN** restrict Er:YAG LAI to the disinfection phase only; do not use high-power laser in the second (regenerative) step
**BECAUSE** Er:YAG LAI poses risk of irrigant extrusion in immature apices, and biostimulation (LLLT/PBM) — not high-power laser — is supported for the regenerative phase [[PMID:40287048]]

---

#### 4c. Materials & Instrumentation

| Category | Specification |
|---|---|
| **Irrigants — primary** | 2–3% NaOCl · volume not standardized in evidence base · deliver until effluent clear |
| **Chelating agent** | 17% EDTA · 4 × 15 s LAI cycles [[PMID:40135760]] [[PMID:41389357]] |
| **Er:YAG SWEEPS tip** | 300 μm radial-firing tip · 50 mJ, 25 Hz, 1 W, 300 μs · fluence 71.4 J/cm² [[PMID:40135760]] |
| **aPDT photosensitiser** | Phenothiazinium salt · 1–5 min pre-irradiation contact · wavelength-matched diode [[PMID:41388259]] |
| **LLLT parameters** | 635 nm · 400 mW · 2 J/point · 4 J/cm² · 4 sessions [[PMID:40135760]] |

---

*Knowing which systems exist and how to deploy them is necessary but not sufficient — the decisive question is whether lasers actually eliminate the pathogens responsible for treatment failure. Module 3 examines the microbial evidence directly.*

---

## Module 3 — Efficacy against endodontic pathogens and biofilms

**The microbial challenge in root canal disinfection** centres on polymicrobial biofilms harbouring species such as *Enterococcus faecalis*, *Streptococcus* spp., *Actinomyces* spp., and *Peptostreptococcus micros*, identified by MALDI-TOF spectrometry across 80 species from six phyla in retreatment and periapical disease cases [[PMID:37925063]]. Fungi — predominantly *Candida* spp. — appear in approximately 9.11% of endodontic infections (weighted mean prevalence from 2,003 samples across 39 studies), rising to 16% in secondary infections when molecular methods are used [[PMID:34293029]]. Complete eradication by chemomechanical preparation alone is consistently unachieved across all pathogen groups [[PMID:36156313]].

**Laser-activated irrigation (LAI): overall clinical picture.** The highest-tier evidence for LAI comes from a 2026 umbrella review of nine systematic reviews (PROSPERO-registered; AMSTAR-2 assessed) covering Er:YAG, Er,Cr:YSGG, Nd:YAG, and diode systems [[PMID:41833582]]. Its conclusion is unequivocal: evidence remains **limited and heterogeneous**, variability in wavelengths and outcome measures prevents definitive conclusions, and LAI should currently be regarded as an adjunct with unproven clinical benefit pending robust standardised trials. This is the lead citation for any claim about LAI's clinical superiority; lower-tier findings below must be interpreted within this ceiling.

**Laser-specific antibacterial mechanisms** vary by wavelength. Nd:YAG laser (1,064 nm) exerts photothermal effects — protein denaturation, cell-membrane disruption, and mixed-species biofilm degradation — and can penetrate dentinal tubules, offering adjunctive value without achieving consistent sterilisation [[PMID:40565094]]. Er:YAG laser activates irrigants via photon-induced photoacoustic streaming (PIPS) and shock wave-enhanced emission photoacoustic streaming (SWEEPS), generating superior bacterial reduction particularly in the apical third and enabling use of lower NaOCl concentrations without sacrificing efficacy [[PMID:40136729]]. In a 3D-printed model study (n=20), Er:YAG LAI (P400FL tip at canal entrance; 25 pps, 50 mJ, 300 μs; 3 × 20 s per canal; 3 mL per 20 s) removed significantly more biofilm-mimicking hydrogel from the entire root canal system than conventional needle irrigation, sonic, or ultrasonic activation (p<0.05) [[PMID:38382735]].

**The literature is currently divided on this topic.** Among the highest-quality Level I sources: the 2026 umbrella review [[PMID:41833582]] concludes LAI benefit is unproven clinically, while a prospective RCT (n=60) found PIPS with 1% NaOCl produced significantly lower post-irrigation ATP values than conventional needle irrigation with the same solution (p<0.001) [[PMID:38431616]], and a separate in vivo study (n=30) found that dual Er,Cr:YSGG (2,780 nm)/diode (940 nm) laser protocols produced significantly lower CFU counts than conventional 2.5% NaOCl + 17% EDTA irrigation [[PMID:38403667]]. The umbrella review [[PMID:41833582]], as the highest-tier synthesis, takes precedence: individual RCTs with surrogate microbiological endpoints cannot yet be translated into confirmed clinical superiority.

**Antimicrobial photodynamic therapy (aPDT): the strongest laser-adjunct evidence base.** A 2025 PROSPERO-registered systematic review with meta-analysis (11 RCTs; ROB-2 assessed; GRADE-rated) found aPDT as an adjunct to chemomechanical irrigation significantly reduced microbial load, with only three of eleven studies at low risk of bias and certainty rated moderate [[PMID:41388259]]. A separate 2023 PROSPERO-registered SR/meta-analysis (8 clinical trials in permanent teeth) confirmed aPDT yields additional microbial reduction over chemomechanical preparation alone (p=0.04; 95% CI −1.72 to −0.05), with superior effect on anaerobic microorganisms (p=0.003) [[PMID:37981598]]. In retreatment specifically, meta-analysis (OR 0.15; 95% CI 0.07–0.32; p<0.0001; GRADE: moderate) supports aPDT efficacy in reducing secondary infection microbial load [[PMID:35840008]].

**Photosensitiser choice matters critically.** An ex-vivo SR/meta-analysis (7 studies, *E. faecalis* in extracted human teeth) found NaOCl+PDT with **methylene blue** significantly outperformed NaOCl alone (SMD=5.64; 95% CI 2.67–8.62; p=0.0002), whereas **toluidine blue** showed no significant additional benefit; high heterogeneity (I²=95%) limits certainty of the pooled estimate [[PMID:41692102]]. Indocyanine green (ICG) paired with infrared diode laser achieved microbial reductions comparable to 2.5% NaOCl positive controls in dual-species *E. faecalis/Candida albicans* biofilms and induced the highest oxidative stress among all tested photosensitisers [[PMID:41465429]] — this rests solely on an in-vitro study of bovine incisors (n=20 per group; Dourado et al., 2025); no RCT or prospective human cohort has evaluated ICG-mediated laser ablation in vivo; treat as provisional pending higher-tier confirmation.

**Diode laser for retreatment.** A 12-month RCT (n=30) using a 980 nm diode laser (320 μm fiber; pulsed mode; 1.5 W; 100 Hz; 20 s per canal in helicoidal movements) achieved 42.44% total microbial reduction and 53.14% *E. faecalis* reduction at the pre-instrumentation stage, and resulted in 45% more healed periapical cases at 12 months versus placebo (p<0.05) [[PMID:36823417]]. The laser did not provide synergistic benefit after full biomechanical preparation, indicating its greatest value is as a pre-shaping adjunct — not a replacement for chemomechanical protocols.

---

### Clinical Application

#### 4a. Procedural Protocol

1. **Complete chemomechanical preparation first.** Shape canals to a minimum apical size 25/.06 using a rotary NiTi system. Irrigate throughout with 2.5% NaOCl (minimum 2 mL per canal per exchange) — chemomechanical preparation is the irreplaceable foundation; laser or aPDT adjuncts cannot compensate for inadequate shaping [[PMID:41388259]] [[PMID:41833582]].

2. **Final EDTA rinse for smear-layer removal.** Irrigate with 17% EDTA, 1 mL per canal, 60 s contact time, to expose dentinal tubules and optimise photosensitiser or irrigant penetration before any laser adjunct is applied [[PMID:38403667]].

3. **If using Er:YAG LAI (PIPS protocol):** Insert P400FL radial-firing tip to canal entrance (not working length). Activate 1% NaOCl (3 mL per canal delivered at 3 mL per 20 s) at 25 pps, 50 mJ, 300 μs for 3 × 20 s cycles per canal [[PMID:38382735]] [[PMID:38431616]]. Fiegler-Rudol et al. (2025) report this concentration is sufficient when paired with PIPS/SWEEPS photoacoustic activation [[PMID:40136729]]; Donnermeyer et al. did not report apical extrusion data for this protocol [[PMID:38382735]].

4. **If using diode laser (980 nm) as a pre-shaping adjunct in retreatment:** After access and canal negotiation but before full biomechanical preparation, insert a 320 μm fiber in helicoidal motion and irradiate in pulsed mode at 1.5 W, 100 Hz for 20 s per canal [[PMID:36823417]]. Irrigate canals with saline between laser passes; the evidence base for this protocol does not specify a volume per pass — use sufficient volume to keep the canal visibly moist (saline volume not reported by Pelozo et al.) [[PMID:36823417]].

5. **If using Er,Cr:YSGG (2,780 nm) + diode (940 nm) dual-laser protocol:** Apply Er,Cr:YSGG intracanal first for biofilm disruption, followed by 940 nm diode irradiation; irrigant vehicle is 17% EDTA [[PMID:38403667]]. Fahim et al. did not specify per-canal fiber diameter or exposure time for each device; consult manufacturer protocol for those parameters [[PMID:38403667]].

6. **If using aPDT:** Apply methylene blue photosensitiser (0.005% aqueous solution as used by Okamoto et al. [[PMID:29510847]]; up to 0.1% as used by Zargar et al. [[PMID:41789272]]) to the canal lumen via fine optical fiber delivery tip; allow 3 min pre-irradiation dark contact time [[PMID:29510847]]. Irradiate with a 660 nm diode laser at 15 J total energy for 6 min, delivered via a 320 μm optical fiber in slow circumferential helicoidal motion [[PMID:26071387]]. Use methylene blue — meta-analysis shows no added benefit from toluidine blue [[PMID:41692102]].

7. **Flush and dry after laser/aPDT.** Irrigate with sterile saline to clear photosensitiser residue before obturation; Garcez et al. report post-aPDT saline irrigation as part of the periapical surgery protocol [[PMID:26071387]]. Paper-point drying to working length is standard endodontic practice; the evidence base for this specific step does not report a specified saline volume.

8. **Obturate or place inter-appointment dressing.** For single-visit cases, proceed to obturation. For multi-visit high-load cases, place calcium hydroxide inter-appointment dressing. Intracanal medicaments (calcium hydroxide, triple antibiotic paste, double antibiotic paste) did not significantly affect subsequent sealer dentinal tubule penetration across AH Plus, MTA Fillapex, or TotalFill in a study of 120 single-rooted teeth (p>0.05) [[PMID:40713572]].

---

#### 4b. Decision Tree

**IF** the tooth has a primary endodontic infection in a permanent tooth with apical periodontitis and chemomechanical preparation has been completed
**THEN** add aPDT with methylene blue (0.005%–0.1%, 660 nm diode, 15 J/6 min) as an adjunct
**BECAUSE** two PROSPERO-registered SR/meta-analyses confirm statistically significant additional microbial reduction over chemomechanical preparation alone, especially for anaerobes [[PMID:37981598]] [[PMID:41388259]]

**IF** the tooth requires endodontic retreatment with a persistent periapical lesion and a 980 nm diode laser is available
**THEN** perform diode laser irradiation (320 μm fiber, 1.5 W, pulsed mode, 100 Hz, 20 s per canal, helicoidal motion) after access and canal negotiation, before full biomechanical preparation
**BECAUSE** a 12-month RCT demonstrated 42.44% microbial reduction at this pre-shaping stage and 45% more healed periapical cases at follow-up versus placebo [[PMID:36823417]]

**IF** complex anatomy (isthmus, lateral canals, or curved canals ≥60° curvature) is identified on pre-operative CBCT
**THEN** select Er:YAG LAI (PIPS protocol: P400FL tip, 25 pps, 50 mJ, 300 μs, 3 × 20 s, 1% NaOCl) over conventional needle irrigation or ultrasonic activation
**BECAUSE** LAI removed significantly more biofilm-mimicking hydrogel from isthmus and apical structures (p<0.05) in a 3D-printed model study [[PMID:38382735]], though no in-vivo RCT has yet confirmed this finding in complex anatomy; treat as provisional pending higher-tier confirmation

---

*With pathogen-specific evidence now mapped, the final module translates this into clinical outcome expectations — addressing periapical healing rates, post-operative pain management, complications, and the special scenarios of pulp preservation and endo-perio lesions.*

---

## Module 4 — Clinical outcomes, complications, and treatment success

**Periapical healing: what laser adjuncts actually deliver**

The highest-tier question in this module is whether adding laser-based adjuncts to chemomechanical preparation improves the healing of apical periodontitis (AP). Meire et al., 2023, a PROSPERO-registered systematic review of 14 clinical studies (13 RCTs, 1 cohort), assessed aPDT, diode laser irradiation, Nd:YAG, Er;Cr:YSGG, ozone, and UAI [[PMID:36156804]]. Meta-analysis for radiographic healing at 12 months was achievable only for UAI (2 studies), yielding no statistically significant difference over controls [[PMID:36156804]]. GRADE assessment rated diode laser evidence as very low certainty and PDT/UAI as low certainty [[PMID:36156804]]. The authors' conclusion is unambiguous: **there is insufficient evidence to recommend any adjunctive laser therapy for the treatment of AP in permanent teeth** [[PMID:36156804]].

At the RCT level, Doğan et al., 2024 (n = 56, 12-month CBCT follow-up) compared LAI-SWEEPS, PUI, MDA, and a control group in single-rooted mandibular teeth with periapical index ≥ 3 [[PMID:38878107]]. All groups showed significant volumetric reduction from baseline (p = 0.001) [[PMID:38878107]]. CBCT lesion volume reduction ranked: SWEEPS 86.9% > PUI 85.4% > MDA 80.4% > control 74.5%, but no between-group difference reached statistical significance (p > 0.05) [[PMID:38878107]]. This pattern — numerical advantage without statistical superiority — is characteristic of the current evidence base.

**Postoperative pain: where laser evidence is strongest**

**The literature is currently divided on this topic.** Meire et al., 2023 found no significant reduction in pain prevalence at 7 days for aPDT (3-study meta-analysis) or diode laser irradiation (2-study meta-analysis) versus controls [[PMID:36156804]]. Conversely, Luo et al., 2024 (22 RCTs, n = 892) reported significantly reduced pain scores for LLLT (SMD = −0.86 at 24 h; SMD = −0.64 at 48 h), diode LAI (SMD = −0.27 at 48 h), and aPDT (SMD = −1.12 at 24 h), with aPDT also reducing pain incidence (pooled RR = 0.47) [[PMID:39287434]]. The larger and more recent meta-analysis by Sabeti et al., 2026 (7 RCTs, n = 490) demonstrated that LAI significantly reduces postoperative pain versus UAI (SMD = −0.58; 95% CI −0.94 to −0.22; p = 0.0016), with pulsed Er:YAG modalities producing the greatest effect at 24–48 h (PIPS SMD = −1.10; SWEEPS SMD = −1.57); diode LAI showed no significant effect (SMD = 0.03) [[PMID:40818665]]. Das et al., 2025 (11 RCTs, meta-analysis) confirmed aPDT significantly reduced VAS pain at 24 h (SMD = −1.21) and 72 h (SMD = −0.63) versus controls [[PMID:41388259]]. The higher-quality and larger pooled studies favour pulsed Er:YAG LAI and aPDT for pain reduction; diode irradiation alone shows inconsistent benefit. The 810-nm semiconductor laser RCT by Jian, 2025 (n = 202) found that combined LAI + LLLT produced the lowest 14-day VAS scores and analgesic consumption (0.53 ± 0.74 tablets) compared with controls (significantly more, p < 0.001) [[PMID:41063319]].

**Complications and safety**

No laser-related adverse events at a clinically significant rate were reported in the RCTs reviewed. Kolberg-Babrzyńska et al., 2025 (n = 40) documented that Er:YAG LAI at 50 mJ, 25 Hz, 1 W, 300 μs with a 300-μm tip produced statistically lower VAS scores at days 1, 2, and 4 post-retreatment and significantly greater periapical lesion reduction at 6 months (mean PL size: test group 1.55 ± 0.51 mm vs. control group 1.95 ± 0.71 mm; p < 0.05), without adverse events [[PMID:40135760]]. Doğan et al. did not report irrigant extrusion or thermal damage in any group [[PMID:38878107]].

**Pulp-preservation outcomes with laser adjuncts**

For vital pulp therapy, Swetha et al., 2024 (n = 86, 18-month follow-up) compared GaAlAs 980-nm diode laser hemostasis with 2.5% NaOCl hemostasis in full coronal pulpotomy of permanent molars with symptomatic irre
